title: Perfect resonance and fragile localization suppression in correlated disordered chains
abstract: Spatial correlations can suppress scattering in disordered chains and produce perfectly transmitting resonances. The practical value of this protection, however, depends not on the resonance peak itself but on the width of the surrounding transmission window and its sensitivity to local ordering errors. We show that a resonance can remain exactly transparent at its center while arbitrarily rare adjacent-swap errors restore an inverse localization length proportional to the square of the energy detuning. For lossless single-channel chains assembled from independent blocks of fixed length and composition, this positive quadratic term is guaranteed by a local scattering invariant and holds for every arrangement and every fixed swap probability between zero and one. With exact tuning and matched contacts, the central transmission remains unity. A microscopic quantum chain exhibits both higher-order suppression of scattering in the ideal recursive arrangement and the predicted response to local exchanges. These results reveal a limitation of spatial ordering that is invisible to a measurement at the resonance alone: spatial ordering protects the resonance peak, not the transport around it. The effect can therefore be tested experimentally by measuring transmission spectra before and after exchanges, without identifying microscopic defects.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes how spatial correlations in disordered quantum chains can induce perfect transmission resonances. The key finding is that while the central resonance remains robust against local swaps, the surrounding transport spectrum is degraded, showing a quadratic dependence on energy detuning. This suggests that structural ordering protects the resonance peak but not the overall transport properties.
main_problem: The study investigates how spatial correlations in disordered quantum chains can create perfectly transmitting resonances, and critically, how this protection fails when subjected to local ordering errors like neighboring cell swaps.
main_result: While perfect ordering ensures a central resonance peak remains perfectly transparent, local swaps restore an inverse localization length proportional to the square of the energy detuning, proving that spatial ordering protects the peak but not the surrounding transport.
method: The analysis uses transfer matrix methods, graph theory concepts (minimum spanning-tree weight), and high-precision numerical calculations to derive lower bounds for the localization rate induced by local disorder.
model_or_system: The model is a correlated disordered quantum chain, built from blocks of fixed length and composition, analyzed using single-channel transfer matrices derived from a microscopic Hamiltonian involving core orbitals and auxiliary dimers.
key_observables: Transmission spectrum ($T_N(E)$), localization rate ($\gamma(E)$), and the quadratic coefficient ($\Gamma_2$) describing the energy dependence of scattering.
important_parameters: Swap probability ($p_{sw}$), energy detuning ($E$), and the length of the chain ($N$).
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses on errors that involve swapping two neighboring cells without changing the overall count of each cell type.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate that local exchanges preserve the resonance peak transmission ($T_N(0)=1$) but alter the surrounding spectrum, and they compare the derived quadratic localization coefficient ($\Gamma_2$) against rigorous theoretical lower bounds.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the perfect resonance condition via spatial correlations, to quantifying the effect of local swaps using transfer matrices and graph theory, and finally confirming the quadratic energy dependence of the restored localization rate through detailed numerical and analytical bounds.
why_interesting: The finding that local disorder affects the transport *around* a resonance, rather than the resonance itself, provides a novel diagnostic tool for characterizing quantum transport in disordered materials that is sensitive to local structural integrity.
